paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 1. English translation of source: “‘Our teachers taught: For three transgressions women die at the time of childbirth. All three have their basis in the Torah: niddah, as it is written, ‘If a woman has a flow [of blood]’; challah, ‘The first of your dough’; and the lighting of a lamp, as it is written, ‘You shall call Shabbos a delight’—this refers to kindling the Shabbos lamp. If you should say that one might sit in darkness, that is not delight, for those who descend to Gehinnom are judged in darkness, as it says, ‘A land of deepest gloom, like darkness.’’ The Midrash continues: ‘Why were women commanded concerning these three mitzvos? ... She caused [Adam] to die and shed his blood ... She defiled the challah of the world ... She extinguished Adam’s lamp, as it is written, ‘The soul of man is the lamp of the Lord’; therefore she must attend to kindling the lamp.’” Context and connection: The source develops both sides of Rav Tzadok’s argument: the three practices address the loss introduced by the first sin, while light is the positive image of Shabbos restoration. The relevant lamp passage occurs in Noach 1 in the commonly indexed Sefaria edition; Rav Tzadok's printed numbering differs.

paragraphs.text: Genesis 1:2; Midrash Tanchuma, Bo 2. English translation of source: “Genesis 1:2: ‘The earth was unformed and empty, darkness was over the face of the deep, and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.’ Midrash Tanchuma, Bo 2: ‘Rabbi Nechemiah said: [The darkness of Egypt came] from the darkness of Gehinnom, for it is said, ‘A land of thick gloom, like darkness, of deathly shadow and no order.’ ... With what are the wicked covered in Gehinnom? With darkness. Just as an earthenware jar is covered with an earthenware lid, so these wicked ones, whose deeds are in the dark, are covered by the Holy One, blessed be He, with the deep, which is darkness, as it says: ‘And darkness was upon the face of the deep.’ This is Gehinnom.’” Context and connection: In the verse, darkness precedes creation’s illumination. In the Midrash it becomes a moral image: a person concealed in wrongdoing encounters concealment. Rav Tzadok juxtaposes this with the contrary possibility that divine judgment may awaken recognition and thereby itself be experienced as light.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 54a. English translation of source: “‘This is no difficulty: one statement concerns our fire and one concerns the fire of Gehinnom. Our fire [was created] at the close of Shabbos; the fire of Gehinnom, on the eve of Shabbos. But was the fire of Gehinnom created on the eve of Shabbos? Was it not taught that seven things were created before the world: the Torah, repentance, the Garden of Eden, Gehinnom, the Throne of Glory, the Sanctuary, and the name of the Messiah? ... Rabbi Yose says: The fire created by the Holy One, blessed be He, on the second day never goes out, as it says, ‘Their fire shall not be quenched.’ ... Why was ‘for it was good’ not said on the second day? Because the fire of Gehinnom was created then.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok deliberately focuses on the expression ‘the light of Gehinnom.’ He is not denying its punitive aspect. He argues that for one who accepts the truth of the judgment, the confrontation can illuminate what was previously hidden. The paradox depends on distinguishing revelatory light from the comfort of an ordinary flame.

paragraphs.text: Further parallel — Tiferet Yosef, Bereshit 2, paragraphs 5, 7, 9 (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library): ““A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day: It is good to give thanks to Hashem” (Psalms 92:1-2). My revered grandfather, my master and teacher, of blessed memory, explained regarding this that the ultimate purpose of the creation of heaven and earth is the Sabbath day. Meaning, during the six workdays, man acts and toils, and it appears to him that he himself is piercing the concealment and recognizing the revelation of the Kingdom of Heaven in the world. And afterwards, on the Sabbath day, man realizes: “What was the world lacking? Rest; the Sabbath came, rest came” (Rashi on Genesis 2:2) — meaning, he recognizes that even the very strength to toil was entirely granted by Hashem, and he recognizes that in truth, from the perspective of Hashem, all is without limit and without boundary; and that these boundaries which Hashem instituted were solely because He desired to bestow good upon His creations, wishing that the Jew should coronate Hashem through free choice, actively choosing the good and despising the bad. For had the revelation of the Kingdom of Heaven been completely explicit, there would be no free will whatsoever, as all would clearly recognize that it is impossible to flee from the Source of Life; therefore Hashem established these limitations.”

paragraphs.text: Sotah 5a, with Tosafos ad loc.. English translation of source: “Sotah 5a: ‘Rabbi Alexandri said: Anyone who possesses haughtiness—even a light wind stirs him, for it is written, ‘The wicked are like the troubled sea, for it cannot rest.’ And if the sea, which contains so many quarter-measures [of water], is stirred by a slight wind, then a human being, in whose body there is only a quarter-log of blood, all the more so!’ Tosafos, s.v. ‘A person who has only a quarter-log of blood’: ‘Rabbeinu Chananel explains: This is the clear blood upon which the heart is sustained; its weight is only twenty-five sela, which is a quarter of a log.’” Context and connection: This distinction serves a specific purpose in his argument. The bodily blood of the organs represents nefesh, whereas the refined vitality of the heart corresponds to ruach. Accordingly he connects the niddah-related repair to the place where inner emotional and spiritual life is situated. The precise physiological language belongs to the traditional exegetical model, not modern anatomy.

Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: Had Israel observed two Shabbosos according to their laws, they would have been redeemed immediately, as it says, ‘So says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep My Shabbosos,’ and afterward it says, ‘I shall bring them to My holy mountain.’’” Context and connection: The sugya speaks of collective redemption, but Rav Tzadok broadens its spiritual logic: even for a single person, faithful Shabbos observance interrupts the weekday reign of the yetzer hara and opens an experience of personal redemption.

paragraphs.text: Further parallel — Takanat HaShavin 15 [paragraph 209] (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library): “And at Marah they were commanded concerning the Shabbos (Shabbos 87b), as they stated [in Perek Rabi Akiva, Shabbos 118b]; for it is known that on Shabbos indulgence is a mitzvah, since all physical desires are then elevated into holiness. And this is the bitter element that sweetened the bitter: that through the bitterness of this world one merits the World that is entirely good and delightful; and likewise the six days of action and Shabbos which is a foretaste of the World to Come;”

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Takanat HaShavin 6:49 (§2): “For the matter of his sale [was thus]: the tribes did not [yet] know that Yaakov’s “bed was whole,” and thought that “dross” had issued from him too, as from Avraham and Yitzchak [Ishmael and Esav]; and they “imagined” [this] of Yosef, since they saw him “desiring to rule over them.” is the essential Name of Hashem, comprising all the vitality bestowed into creation — which is the ‘middle line’ [kav emtzai] of all creation. And Yosef, too, holds fast to this rung, for ‘the radiance of his countenance resembled his father’s’; and the tzaddik is the ‘guardian of the covenant,’ the rung of Yosef, in whom the [Divine] Name prevails.”” Connection to this note: In Takanat HaShavin 6:49 (§2), Rav Tzadok develops the parallel foundation illuminating Exodus 12:2 and the teaching in Peri Tzadik, Noach 5 — Shabbat Lights and the Restoration of the Soul.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 54:14–16: “And this was the very reason their redemption was hidden: because they ruined in practical action the root of unity through baseless hatred, they forfeited the primordial sanctity of the Temple and were exiled. So in the future redemption: Israel's return to unity will be achieved through their preliminary spiritual clarifications, as in Tanchuma (Nitzavim 1): “Israel is not redeemed until they form a single unified band: ‘In those days the children of Israel shall come, they and the children of Judah together’; when bound together they welcome the Shechinah.”” Connection to this note: This Beis Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 54:14–16 sheds direct light on Exodus 12:2 and Rav Tzadok's exposition in Peri Tzadik, Noach 5 — Shabbat Lights and the Restoration of the Soul.
